text: Lesson 32 confirmed Meridian Freight's instance has a task table and the ITSM applications built on top of it. Now you document exactly how they connect, starting with the task hierarchy itself — the structure that everything else in this instance's service desk is built on.

Open System Definition, Tables, find incident, and check its Extends table field. It reads task. Do the same for problem and for change_request, and you've just verified — rather than assumed — the hierarchy this entire ITSM suite is actually built on, which is the first line of your write-up.

Next, open the Incident table's own dictionary: System Definition, Dictionary, filtered to incident. A dictionary entry shows a field's column name, its label, and its type at a glance. You don't need all hundred-plus fields — three on Incident are worth a line each in your documentation.

Priority is a Choice field — a fixed, predefined list of values, which is exactly what makes reporting on it reliable. Caller_id is a Reference field — it stores a sys_id pointing at sys_user, not a typed name, which is why confirming that base table in Lesson 32 mattered. Work_notes is a Journal field — it appends every new entry rather than overwriting the last one.

On a populated Incident record, expect at least one related list showing Affected CIs, pointing back at cmdb_ci — proof that base table from Lesson 32 isn't sitting empty. Depending on configuration, you'd also expect related lists tying the incident back to any linked Problem or Change record.

Three short sections cover the write-up: the confirmed table hierarchy, the three field types on Incident with one line of justification each, and the related lists found on a real populated record. That's a usable capstone document. Lesson 34 closes out the entire course.
